title: 二号六号拿混钥匙  (Keys Two and Six Swapped)

segments.t: Back at the front desk, Chen points his carpenter pencil at two empty brass hooks on the wooden board while Zhou blinks at his forehead and Qing skids to a stop. Listen first.
老陈，快汇报！中午接电话的时候哪几把房门钥匙发乱了？
看我这本纸账本：两位年轻徒步客订的是一楼二号房。
对呀，特别礼貌的两位徒步客——还有位拎花纹帽盒的文静女士订了六号房！
那你跟小晴说说，发二号和六号牌子的时候，你的眼镜架在哪儿呢？
哎哟……倒过来看，二像五，不对——模糊起来二和六简直一模一样！
难不成徒步客把双肩包拎去六号房，而帽盒去了二号房？！
算你走运，老板，两位客人把行李放在门外就出门吃午饭去了！
真的吗？！两边客人都还没开错门，也没翻出一件衬衫？！
两分钟前我在大门口刚跟他们擦肩而过，他们正打听上哪儿买午饭热汤呢。
老陈，你这双火眼金睛太管用了——咱们能立刻把行李换回来吗？
还在每间房门口的小桌上留张工整的欢迎便条，写明正确的挂钩号！
小晴，拿上总钥匙圈；你拿帽盒，我扛那两个双肩包。
Now let's go through it line by line with the English translation.
老陈，快汇报！中午接电话的时候哪几把房门钥匙发乱了？
'Report, Chen! Which room keys got mixed up during the noon phone call?' Keys take the slender counter "ba" ("na ji ba yaoshi"), and "fa luan le" means handed out in the wrong order.
看我这本纸账本：两位年轻徒步客订的是一楼二号房。

'Look at my paper ledger: two young hikers booked Room Two on the first floor.' "Tubuke" blends "tubu" ("on foot/hiking") + "ke" ("guest/traveler") for hikers, and "ding de shi" highlights what they booked.
对呀，特别礼貌的两位徒步客——还有位拎花纹帽盒的文静女士订了六号房！

'Yes, such polite hikers—and a quiet lady carrying a floral hatbox booked Room Six!' Carrying something by a handle takes "lin" ("lin huawen maohe"), while "wenjing" describes a gentle, quiet-mannered guest.
那你跟小晴说说，发二号和六号牌子的时候，你的眼镜架在哪儿呢？
'Now tell Qing where your glasses were sitting when you handed out tags Two and Six.' "Genshuo" ("tell someone") in "gen Xiaoqing shuoshuo" invites a confession, while "paizi" means a room key tag.
哎哟……倒过来看，二像五，不对——模糊起来二和六简直一模一样！

'Oh dear... upside down two looks like five, no—when everything's blurry, two and six look almost identical!' "Mohu qilai" means "once things turn blurry," and "yimo yiyang" is the lively expression for "exactly alike."
难不成徒步客把双肩包拎去六号房，而帽盒去了二号房？！

'Don't tell me the hikers hauled their backpacks to Room Six while the hatbox went to Room Two?!' "Shuangjianbao" literally means "two-shoulder bag" (backpack), contrasting with the single-handled hatbox ("maohe").
算你走运，老板，两位客人把行李放在门外就出门吃午饭去了！

'Lucky break for you, boss—both guests left their bags outside the doors and headed out for lunch!' "Suan ni zouyun" means "consider yourself lucky," and "chumen" ("step out the gate") naturally covers going out for a meal.
真的吗？！两边客人都还没开错门，也没翻出一件衬衫？！

'Really?! Neither guest unlocked the wrong door or unpacked a single shirt yet?!' "Kai cuo men" puts "cuo" ("wrong") right after "kai" ("open") to show an action done by mistake, like opening the wrong door.
两分钟前我在大门口刚跟他们擦肩而过，他们正打听上哪儿买午饭热汤呢。

'Two minutes ago I passed right by them at the gate asking where to grab hot lunch soup.' Idiom "cajian" (brush shoulders) vividly pictures passing someone at the gate, while asking around for local tips is "dating".
老陈，你这双火眼金睛太管用了——咱们能立刻把行李换回来吗？

'Chen, those sharp eyes of yours are pure gold—can we swap the bags back right now?' Classic folk phrase "huoyan" + "jinjing" (literally "fiery golden eyes") praises keen eyesight, and "huan huilai" means swapping items back.
还在每间房门口的小桌上留张工整的欢迎便条，写明正确的挂钩号！

'And leave a neat welcome note on each door table explaining the right hook number!' Small note slips take the flat counter "zhang" ("yi zhang ... biantiao"), and "xieming" means writing something down clearly.
小晴，拿上总钥匙圈；你拿帽盒，我扛那两个双肩包。

'Grab the master key ring, Qing; you take the hatbox, and I'll shoulder the two backpacks.' "Zong yaoshi quan" names the master key ring ("zong" = overall/master), while "kang" means hoisting heavy packs onto one's shoulder.
Now let's listen to the whole conversation one last time.

Thanks to lunch soup down Wutong Lane, Qing and Chen have fifteen minutes to put every bag at the right door! See you upstairs next time.
明天见！
